frictionVectors.title: European energy bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over hydrocarbons and pipeline infrastructure, but European buyers are pressing for flexibility, lower prices, and reduced long-term dependence. Competition from LNG suppliers constrains Algiers's leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara and Sahel alignment
frictionVectors.details: Algeria's support for Sahrawi self-determination and its security posture in the Sahel continue to strain relations with Morocco and some external partners, complicating regional infrastructure and trade integration.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The rail corridor linking Angola to the Copperbelt is attracting US, European, Chinese, and Gulf interest. External financing and operators could improve connectivity while limiting Luanda's practical control over strategic logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and upstream dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues remain central to state capacity, while foreign firms and creditors retain significant influence over production, financing, and infrastructure. Declining output and debt-service pressures constrain sovereign bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Niger border and port disruption
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger remain vulnerable to border closures, sanctions spillovers, and disputes over access to regional trade routes. Dependence on the Port of Cotonou makes Benin sensitive to political decisions beyond its borders.

frictionVectors.title: Coastal counterinsurgency dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rising militant activity near the northern frontier is increasing reliance on foreign intelligence, training, and security assistance. Expanded external support may protect corridors but can narrow domestic control over security priorities.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is using its market importance and political leverage to secure greater value from diamond extraction and marketing arrangements. The central risk is that prolonged disputes or weak global demand could reduce revenues and investment.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals financing gap
frictionVectors.details: Lithium, copper, and other mineral projects attract foreign investors seeking supply-chain access, but Botswana must balance rapid development against environmental safeguards and local beneficiation. Limited domestic processing capacity remains a sovereignty constraint.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector nationalization pressure
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state control, local processing, and revenue capture from gold while challenging foreign mining arrangements. Production disruptions, regulatory uncertainty, and insecurity may deter investment and reduce actual state returns.

frictionVectors.title: Security dependence and territorial access
frictionVectors.details: Expanded cooperation with Russian-linked security actors has reduced reliance on some Western partners but created new external dependencies. Persistent jihadist violence continues to limit state control over mining zones, roads, and border infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda–DRC border tensions
frictionVectors.details: Burundi remains exposed to armed-group activity and regional rivalry around eastern DRC. Border insecurity constrains trade and gives neighboring powers leverage over Bujumbura.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector opacity
frictionVectors.details: Gold and other mineral exports remain vulnerable to informal channels and external brokerage. Limited state capacity reduces Burundi's ability to capture full value from its resources.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime security and narcotics routes
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's position between West Africa, Europe, and the Americas makes its waters important for counter-narcotics operations. Enforcement relies substantially on foreign intelligence, funding, and naval support.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and connectivity dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tourism, imported fuel, and externally financed ports and digital infrastructure leave the islands exposed to outside economic shocks. Diversification is improving but remains structurally limited.

highlights: Oil, gas, and mining remain externally intermediated

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone conflict and separatism
frictionVectors.details: Persistent violence in the Northwest and Southwest regions weakens state control and disrupts transport, agriculture, and local commerce. External humanitarian and diplomatic involvement remains significant.

frictionVectors.title: Resource and pipeline dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbons and emerging mining projects depend on foreign capital, technical operators, and regional export corridors. The Chad–Cameroon pipeline gives external partners lasting influence over revenue flows and infrastructure security.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security and mining involvement
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel and commercial networks remain central to regime protection and access to gold and diamond opportunities. This arrangement limits transparency and weakens the state's bargaining position over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Armed-group control of resource zones
frictionVectors.details: Rebel and criminal networks continue to influence transport corridors and mining areas outside the capital. Weak infrastructure makes national regulation and formal revenue collection difficult.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan conflict and refugee pressure
frictionVectors.details: War in Sudan has intensified insecurity along Chad's eastern frontier and increased humanitarian and logistical burdens. Cross-border armed-group activity could further divert state resources from development and resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: Oil corridor and foreign leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chad's oil sector depends on foreign operators and the export pipeline through Cameroon, limiting national control over pricing, logistics, and technical capacity. Oil concentration also reinforces a centralized security model and exposes public finances to external market conditions.

frictionVectors.title: French Control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, sustaining Comoros' central sovereignty dispute and limiting its effective control over surrounding maritime space. The issue remains a persistent source of diplomatic friction and domestic pressure.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence and Fisheries
frictionVectors.details: Remittances, foreign aid, and imported energy underpin the economy, while limited enforcement capacity leaves fisheries and maritime resources vulnerable to outside exploitation.

frictionVectors.title: M23 Conflict and Regional Intervention
frictionVectors.details: The conflict in eastern DRC continues to undermine state control over territory, transport routes, and mining zones, with Rwanda-linked forces and other armed networks central to the security crisis.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Governance
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt remain central to global energy supply chains, but weak oversight, opaque contracts, and inadequate infrastructure allow foreign firms and intermediaries to capture disproportionate value.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: State revenue and export capacity remain heavily tied to offshore oil, leaving sovereignty and fiscal stability exposed to price cycles and the bargaining power of international energy firms.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-Resources Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure and financing deepen connectivity but can constrain policy autonomy through debt, procurement dependence, and opaque resource-linked arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Sovereignty and Foreign Processing
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire is strengthening local processing and producer regulation, but multinational buyers still hold substantial influence over pricing, logistics, and access to higher-value segments.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea Security
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port and offshore energy assets remain exposed to piracy, trafficking, and regional instability, requiring continued reliance on external security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Base Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, France, Japan, and other powers use Djibouti's facilities, generating revenue and diplomatic leverage while limiting the space for fully autonomous security policy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's ports and rail links are vital to Ethiopia but remain vulnerable to debt pressure, competition among foreign operators, and disputes over infrastructure control, particularly involving Chinese financing.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Gulf capital dependence
frictionVectors.details: External financing, Gulf investment, and IMF-linked reforms constrain Cairo's policy space over strategic assets and foreign-exchange management.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains unresolved, leaving Egypt exposed to perceived risks to downstream water availability and agricultural stability.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon decline
frictionVectors.details: Falling oil and gas output reduces fiscal room while foreign technical and investment partners retain importance in sustaining offshore production.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Large state projects and hydrocarbon-linked contracts remain vulnerable to external commercial pressure and limited public oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea strategic competition
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to shipping routes attract competing Gulf, regional, and wider international interest, increasing pressure on Asmara's sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Border and conscription tensions
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved relationship with Ethiopia and indefinite national service continue to drive sanctions risk, isolation, and external criticism.

frictionVectors.title: Economic reliance on South Africa
frictionVectors.details: Trade, customs revenue, energy links, and supply chains remain heavily tied to South Africa, limiting Mbabane's strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Political reform pressure
frictionVectors.details: Persistent demands for democratic reform create friction with external partners and complicate access to development finance and investment.

frictionVectors.title: Nile diplomacy confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD expands Ethiopia's control over its electricity and water infrastructure but continues to generate acute tensions with Egypt and Sudan.

frictionVectors.title: External finance and security pressure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, foreign-exchange shortages, and internal conflicts increase reliance on international lenders and limit Addis Ababa's freedom of action.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Oil Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The post-coup authorities are seeking greater state participation and transparency in oil, manganese, and iron-ore assets. Contract reviews could unsettle established foreign operators and reduce near-term investor confidence.

frictionVectors.title: External Security and Infrastructure Influence
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is diversifying longstanding French security and commercial ties while engaging new partners, including Gulf and Asian investors. The transition creates uncertainty around port, logistics, and defense arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Cross-Border Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia remains heavily dependent on Senegal-linked transport, electricity, trade, and security networks. This improves connectivity but limits Banjul's leverage over critical infrastructure and regional policy.

frictionVectors.title: Industrial Fishing and Coastal Livelihoods
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-linked fishing fleets and opaque licensing continue to strain local fisheries and enforcement capacity. Resource depletion risks social unrest and reinforces dependence on external food and revenue systems.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions and Illegal Gold
frictionVectors.details: Foreign mining capital remains essential, while illegal and environmentally destructive gold extraction erodes state authority and fiscal control. Efforts to formalize artisanal mining face entrenched local and external commercial networks.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Fiscal Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed reforms and Chinese-linked infrastructure financing constrain policy space during debt restructuring. Accra is retaining more negotiating leverage, but revenue and project choices remain shaped by creditors and commodity markets.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Foreign-Control Risk
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore corridor is attracting major Chinese, Singaporean, and other international capital, alongside state demands for infrastructure and domestic value capture. The scale of the project could strengthen Guinea's bargaining power while creating long-term dependency on external operators.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite Revenue and Political Transition
frictionVectors.details: Bauxite exports generate substantial foreign earnings but limited local processing and employment relative to the resource base. The military government uses resource nationalism to build legitimacy, while uncertainty over elections and contracts raises governance risk.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Trade Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily dependent on raw cashew exports, with foreign traders and regional intermediaries capturing much of the value. Limited processing capacity leaves producers vulnerable to price manipulation and seasonal liquidity shortages.

frictionVectors.title: Political Instability and Maritime Security
frictionVectors.details: Institutional fragility weakens oversight of ports, fisheries, and offshore waters, creating openings for foreign commercial and illicit networks. Regional actors, especially Senegal and the Economic Community of West African States, remain important security and diplomatic buffers.

highlights: Debt diplomacy narrows room for maneuver
Ports and power remain strategic leverage points

frictionVectors.title: External debt and infrastructure financing
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is balancing IMF-backed fiscal discipline with Chinese, Gulf, and Western financing. Debt-service pressures constrain independent control over major transport and energy projects.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu and coastal corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu port and related corridors remain exposed to regional security risks and competing foreign commercial interests. Their strategic value creates pressure to accommodate outside partners while local benefits remain contested.

highlights: Water exports deepen dependence on Pretoria

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: Water revenues and infrastructure are tied closely to South African demand and financing. The arrangement provides essential income but limits Lesotho's bargaining power over its most strategic natural resource.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and transport vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho remains dependent on South African grids, roads, and commercial access. This dependence makes domestic resource policy sensitive to Pretoria's infrastructure and regulatory decisions.

highlights: Iron ore concessions shape national leverage
Ports and rail corridors attract competing interests

frictionVectors.title: Mining concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and other mineral projects are dominated by foreign operators whose capital and technical capacity remain difficult to replace. Liberia gains employment and revenue, but concession terms constrain sovereign control over deposits and logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail corridor control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-linked mining and shipping interests retain influence over transport infrastructure serving the mineral economy. Weak domestic fiscal and regulatory capacity limits Liberia's ability to capture more value locally.

highlights: Oil remains divided by rival power centers
Foreign security patrons protect competing access

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented control of oil infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Rival authorities and armed groups continue to influence fields, export terminals, and production decisions. Disruptions and opaque revenue arrangements undermine the National Oil Corporation's effective sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military and commercial competition
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, and other external actors retain security and political influence through competing Libyan networks. Their involvement links infrastructure protection and energy access to a broader contest over Libya's sovereignty.

highlights: Nickel and cobalt projects test resource sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-controlled mining value chains
frictionVectors.details: Large nickel, cobalt, and ilmenite operations depend heavily on foreign capital, technology, and export markets. Madagascar receives investment and employment, but environmental costs and limited domestic processing weaken local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Power and logistics bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity and weak transport networks increase dependence on external project finance and private infrastructure. These constraints reduce the state's leverage over strategic mining and agricultural corridors.

frictionVectors.title: External control of mining expansion
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors are positioning for Malawi's uranium, rare-earth and niobium potential as the government seeks capital and export revenue. Weak fiscal capacity limits Lilongwe's bargaining power over contracts, local processing and environmental safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: IMF-linked infrastructure constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and fuel shortages constrain public investment and increase reliance on external lenders. Transport and electricity bottlenecks continue to weaken sovereign control over resource development.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is forcing higher state participation and revised fiscal terms on major gold operators, creating sustained friction with foreign mining companies. The policy may increase public capture of rents but risks reduced investment and production disruption.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security-for-access relationship
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian Africa Corps personnel and political backing has narrowed Mali's strategic options while increasing external influence over security and commercial networks. The arrangement remains controversial amid civilian casualties and weak accountability.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of offshore gas
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with BP and Kosmos is increasing export prospects but leaves Mauritania dependent on foreign operators, technology and infrastructure. Revenue governance and domestic value capture remain central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Resource corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Nouadhibou mining and export system relies heavily on external capital, logistics and Chinese-linked infrastructure partnerships. Expansion could strengthen state revenue while preserving vulnerability to commodity-price and investor decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos settlement implementation
frictionVectors.details: The return of sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago remains strategically important, but the future operating terms of the Diego Garcia facility require careful management. Mauritius must balance territorial claims with the security interests of the United Kingdom and United States.

frictionVectors.title: External exposure in strategic sectors
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius benefits from diversified foreign investment, port development and financial links, but this openness creates exposure to competing Indian, Chinese and Western interests. Port, data and financial infrastructure require continued screening and regulatory capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is using phosphate, fisheries and renewable-energy development in Western Sahara to reinforce its sovereignty claim, while the Polisario Front and legal challenges contest the legitimacy of foreign-linked activity. European and African partners continue to calibrate support to avoid escalation.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Tangier Med, renewable-energy projects and proposed Atlantic corridors increase Moroccan control over regional trade and energy flows. Competition among European, Gulf, Chinese and American partners creates leverage but also pressure over technology, financing and political alignment.

highlights: Cabo Delgado security remains the LNG bottleneck
Gas wealth is advancing faster than local industrial capture

frictionVectors.title: LNG Security and Foreign Operators
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence and dependence on external security support continue to constrain sovereign control over northern gas infrastructure. International energy firms retain major leverage over project timing and revenue flows.

frictionVectors.title: Resource Enclave Risk
frictionVectors.details: LNG, rubies, and other extractive projects generate foreign investment but face persistent concerns over local employment, revenue distribution, and limited domestic processing.

highlights: New hydrocarbons are testing Namibia's resource strategy

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Major offshore discoveries could expand fiscal capacity, but foreign operators and capital currently dominate exploration and technical execution. Namibia is seeking stronger local-content and revenue arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrogen Infrastructure and Water
frictionVectors.details: Green hydrogen projects depend on external finance, export corridors, and substantial water and power infrastructure. Land, environmental, and community-benefit questions could slow implementation.

highlights: Military rule has prioritized resource nationalism
Security and infrastructure constraints limit bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Mining Influence
frictionVectors.details: The junta's distance from Western partners has increased reliance on alternative security relationships, creating risks of opaque concessions and unequal access to uranium, gold, and other resources.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Export Connectivity
frictionVectors.details: Uranium production and other commodities remain vulnerable to political isolation, border disruptions, and weak transport links. Sovereign control is asserted rhetorically but constrained by financing and security dependence.

highlights: Domestic refining is improving energy sovereignty
Oil theft and insecurity still erode state control

frictionVectors.title: Oil Theft and Pipeline Security
frictionVectors.details: Sabotage, crude theft, and insecurity in producing regions continue to reduce public revenues and weaken regulatory authority. International operators remain important to production and technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and Refining Finance
frictionVectors.details: New refining capacity can reduce dependence on imported fuel, but gas monetization and refinery supply chains still rely on complex partnerships, foreign investment, and stable infrastructure.

highlights: Mineral governance is tied to regional security politics
State capacity attracts investment but limits transparency

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Flows
frictionVectors.details: Allegations concerning cross-border support and the movement of tin, tantalum, tungsten, and gold continue to generate pressure from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and external partners. Traceability demands threaten reputational and commercial costs.

frictionVectors.title: Aid, Investment, and Strategic Autonomy
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong state oversight of infrastructure and investment, but depends on external capital, technology, and diplomatic relationships. Development gains coexist with scrutiny over political space and regional policy.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Licensing Uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Sao Tome and Principe is seeking credible offshore exploration while managing overlapping interests in the Nigeria-Sao Tome Joint Development Zone. Limited state capacity and uncertain commercial viability leave the country dependent on foreign operators and partners.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure and budget support remain reliant on Portugal, China, international financial institutions, and other external partners, constraining policy autonomy despite relatively diversified relationships.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Operator Contract Tensions
frictionVectors.details: New oil and gas production has increased Senegal's leverage, but offshore projects remain dependent on international companies, foreign capital, and complex agreements. Efforts to secure greater local content and state participation risk delays and investor friction.

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Governance
frictionVectors.details: The shared Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Mauritania creates revenue-sharing and operational interdependence. Any dispute over allocations, local employment, or project costs could become politically sensitive in both countries.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Fisheries Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles has improved marine governance through protected areas and blue-finance mechanisms, but distant-water fishing access and limited domestic processing leave substantial value captured offshore.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Port, airport, maritime-surveillance, and communications projects attract interest from India, China, France, and other partners. Victoria must balance security assistance and financing without allowing strategic infrastructure to become externally dominated.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mineral Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mineral projects depend heavily on foreign operators, capital, and logistics. Weak bargaining power and limited downstream processing constrain Sierra Leone's ability to retain more value from extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Fisheries Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment in port and transport infrastructure offers needed capacity but raises concerns over concession terms and strategic dependence. Illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing by foreign fleets also erodes coastal revenue and food security.

frictionVectors.title: Turkey-Somalia Offshore Partnership
frictionVectors.details: Turkey's security and energy partnership gives Mogadishu external backing for offshore exploration, but Somalia's weak regulatory capacity and uncertain commercial prospects create risks of opaque contracts and limited domestic capture.

frictionVectors.title: Federal and Regional Maritime Disputes
frictionVectors.details: Disputes involving the federal government, Puntland, Somaliland, and neighboring states complicate control of ports, fisheries, and potential offshore blocks. Persistent al-Shabaab insecurity further limits the state's ability to protect infrastructure and enforce licensing.

frictionVectors.title: MINERALS AND STRATEGIC INVESTMENT
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is balancing Western, Chinese, and Gulf interest in platinum-group metals, manganese, and rare-earth supply chains while seeking greater domestic processing. Investment competition is constrained by regulatory uncertainty and infrastructure weaknesses.

frictionVectors.title: GRID AND PORT CONSTRAINTS
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and rail-port congestion continue to limit sovereign control over mineral exports and industrial capacity. Private-sector participation is expanding, but fiscal and institutional limits slow recovery.

frictionVectors.title: PIPELINE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on Sudanese infrastructure to export oil, leaving revenues exposed to conflict, transit negotiations, and political leverage from Khartoum and regional intermediaries. Production and payment flows remain vulnerable to disruption.

frictionVectors.title: REGIONAL SECURITY INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: Uganda, Sudan, Ethiopia, and other neighboring actors retain influence through security ties, trade routes, and refugee pressures. Weak institutions and elite competition limit the state's ability to convert resource income into sovereign development.

highlights: War fragments control of gold and trade
Red Sea access gains strategic value

frictionVectors.title: GOLD NETWORKS AND EXTERNAL SPONSORS
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling routes are increasingly tied to rival military financing and external commercial networks. Competing foreign relationships are deepening fragmentation rather than strengthening national resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR CONTEST
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan, road corridors, and agricultural zones has become central to war finance and foreign influence. Red Sea stakeholders and regional powers are pursuing access while the central state's territorial authority remains divided.

frictionVectors.title: MINING AND GAS TERMS
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pressing multinational mining and energy companies for local processing, revenue transparency, and stronger state participation. The approach preserves investor access but creates recurring disputes over fiscal terms and project timing.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAIL COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Dar es Salaam and emerging central-corridor links are attracting competition from Gulf, Chinese, Indian, and Western investors. Infrastructure partnerships increase Tanzania's leverage, but also expose strategic assets to long-term foreign dependence.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional logistics hinge

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND TRANSIT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé remains vital to Togo's revenue and regional trade, with foreign operators and investors shaping logistics capacity. Dependence on external capital creates leverage over customs, infrastructure, and corridor priorities.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL SECURITY SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability moving south from Burkina Faso are pressuring northern communities and security spending. Expanded foreign security cooperation may improve state reach while increasing reliance on outside partners.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and migration cooperation give Brussels substantial leverage over Tunisian policy. Domestic resistance to perceived external conditionality complicates implementation.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported gas and electricity, particularly through reliance on Algerian supplies and cross-border infrastructure. Fiscal stress limits its ability to rapidly expand domestic renewable capacity.

highlights: Oil sovereignty faces external financing pressure

frictionVectors.title: EACOP environmental and sanctions exposure
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline remains central to Kampala's resource strategy but faces sustained criticism from environmental groups, Western institutions, and some financiers. Delays or financing constraints could increase dependence on a narrower set of external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure and debt leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese lending and construction remain important to Uganda's transport and energy infrastructure. Debt-servicing obligations and project-linked procurement can reduce Kampala's flexibility in managing strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Copper ownership and taxation disputes
frictionVectors.details: Higher copper demand has strengthened Zambia's negotiating position, but foreign operators still dominate capital, technology, and major production capacity. Disputes over royalties, taxation, and local processing remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Power shortages and dependence on regional transport corridors constrain Zambia's ability to capture more value from copper and critical minerals. New external investment is needed, but may deepen infrastructure and commercial leverage by foreign partners.

highlights: Lithium policy seeks domestic value capture

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of critical minerals
frictionVectors.details: Chinese companies remain prominent in lithium and other mineral projects, providing capital while retaining substantial influence over production and supply chains. Zimbabwe's processing ambitions are constrained by limited power, finance, and technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and payment-system isolation
frictionVectors.details: U.S. and other Western sanctions, alongside broader investor concerns, restrict access to finance and complicate international transactions. This pushes Harare toward a narrower group of external partners and increases bargaining asymmetry.
